title: Freelancing Fundamentals
subtitle: Get the client, agree the terms, get paid
summary: A free course on how freelance work starts and stays alive: where a first client comes from, how to pin down what the job is, how to arrive at a number and say it, what goes in writing before you start, and how to invoice, chase, and handle the client who goes quiet or keeps adding. Nine lessons, written for someone who has never freelanced or has taken a few gigs and been burned.
description: Most people do not lose freelance money because they are bad at the work. They lose it in the gap around the work: a job that was never written down, a rate picked by guessing, a deliverable sent with no invoice behind it, a client who stopped replying. This course covers that gap. You start with the part that has to happen before anything else, which is being findable by somebody who has budget and being chosen when they compare you to four other people. Then the middle, which decides whether the job is profitable: pinning down exactly what you are delivering, what you are not, how many rounds of changes are included, and what the client owes you before you can start, then building a rate out of your own numbers instead of copying a figure from a Facebook group, then putting the whole agreement in writing even when nobody signs anything. The last chapter is delivery and money: running a job so the client is never wondering where it is, sending an invoice that can actually be paid, following up on late payment in steps rather than in one angry message, and the three ways a client relationship comes apart, which are scope creep, silence, and the ending. No rate cards, no platform fee tables, no tax figures. Those change, and a wrong one costs you real money. What you get instead is the arrangement, the questions to ask, and the habit of checking the current number yourself before you rely on it.

Finding clients and writing the first message
Handling scope creep and silent clients

Turn a vague request into a written scope: deliverables, exclusions, revision rounds, dates, and what the client owes you
Build a rate from your own cost floor and unbilled hours, say the number without apologising, and answer a push back on price

lessons.title: What you are actually selling
lessons.content_mdx:
# What you are actually selling

Two people apply for the same job on the same morning.

Joanna writes that she is hardworking, a fast learner, willing to be trained, and open to any kind of task. Reymart writes that he builds and runs weekly product listings for small online sellers, and links to five listings he built for a bag shop in Divisoria.

Reymart is not better at the work. He is easier to buy.

## Nobody hires a general helper

A client with money to spend has a problem in front of them, and they describe it in their own words. Our listings look messy. Nobody answers our emails. Our menu photos are from 2019.

They are not looking for a person who can do anything. They are looking for the answer to that sentence. When your description is a pile of adjectives, the client has to do the work of matching you to their problem, and they will not bother. Somebody further down the list already did it for them.

So the first move in freelancing is not learning another skill. It is naming the one you already have in a way somebody can buy.

## Say it in the buyer's words, with a boundary around it

A service somebody can buy has three parts.

**Who it is for.** Not everyone. "Small online sellers." "Clinics with one receptionist." "Coaches who take bookings over chat."

**What they get.** Something that can be handed over and looked at. Not "social media help", but "twelve captioned posts a month, ready to schedule". Not "admin support", but "your inbox sorted every morning and a short list of what needs your reply".

**Roughly how long it takes.** You do not need a precise figure yet. You need to know whether this is a two-hour job or a two-week one, because you are going to price it later, and you cannot price a shape you have never held.

Test it by saying it out loud as one sentence. I do this, for these people, and what they get is that. If you cannot finish the sentence, you are not ready to message anyone yet.

## Why "I do admin, design, writing and video" fails twice

It fails first as positioning. Four services on one line read as four half-services, and a client comparing you against somebody who does only the thing they need has an easy decision to make.

It fails again as pricing, which is the part beginners do not see coming. A rate is built out of how long a specific job takes you and how many times you have done it. When your offer is "anything", every job is your first job, every estimate is a guess, and the guess will be low. Chapter 2 is about arriving at a number, and it needs a service with edges to work on.

You are allowed to be able to do four things. You are choosing which one goes at the front.

## Choosing it when nobody has paid you yet

Pick where two circles overlap: what you can already do to a standard you would show a stranger, and what you can produce evidence of this week.

Evidence is where people stall, because they are waiting for a client to give them permission. You do not need one.

Build one piece of work against one real business that never hired you. Kaye wanted to shoot menu photos for small food places. She walked into a carinderia in Antipolo she passes every day, bought lunch, photographed it properly at home, and rebuilt their three worst menu images. She sent the shop the files with no invoice and no pitch attached. Whether or not they used them, she now owns a sample about a real business with a real problem, instead of a practice file about nothing.

The other route is one small finished piece of real work for someone you know: your tita's tutorial centre, a cousin's sari-sari store page. Small and finished beats large and imagined.

## What proof looks like

Four things, every time. The artefact itself. What the situation was. What you did. What changed.

"Rebuilt three menu images for a carinderia, using their own dishes, shot at home in daylight" is proof. "Creative and detail-oriented" is an adjective.

Gathering your full inventory of evidence, and turning it into a portfolio a stranger can browse, belongs to the resume and portfolio course. What you need here is one piece, aimed at one kind of buyer, so that your sentence has something standing behind it.

## Before the next lesson

Write your sentence: what you do, who for, and what they get. Then name the one business you will build your sample against, and the date you will finish it.

lessons.content_mdx:
# Where the work actually comes from

Work reaches a freelancer by four routes. Each one costs you something different, and the route that is easiest to start on is the one that keeps the least of you.

## The four routes

**Freelance marketplaces.** You build a profile, buyers post jobs, you send proposals. What you get is buyers who have already decided to hire somebody. What you pay is competition, because your proposal lands beside many others, often from people in other countries working from a different cost floor. You also pay a cut: marketplaces take a share of the money before it reaches you, and some also charge for the ability to apply. Those amounts differ by platform and they change, so read the platform's own fee page before you decide what a job is worth to you, and read it again when something looks different.

**Direct outreach.** You choose businesses that visibly have the problem you solve, and you contact them. Nobody is bidding against you, because there is no post. What you pay is patience, since you are talking to people who were not shopping. This is the slowest route to start and the strongest one to own. The relationship is yours and nothing sits between you and the money.

**Referrals.** Somebody who has seen your work tells somebody else. There is no competition and the trust arrives before you do. What you pay is that you cannot start here. Referrals are an output of finished work, which is why chapter 3 spends its time on delivery.

**Communities and groups.** Facebook groups, chat groups, alumni and parish networks, industry pages where a business owner types "anyone here who can do this?" out loud. Free to join, uneven in quality, and the currency is being visibly useful before you are needed rather than being fastest to comment "PM sent po".

## The marketplace trap

Marketplaces are a sensible place to start. They put buyers in front of you before anybody knows your name.

They are a weak place to stay if every job ends when the job ends. The platform owns the buyer, sets the terms, takes its share, and can change any of that without asking you. A freelancer who works a marketplace for a year and finishes with no repeat client and no referral has bought a year of income and built nothing underneath it.

So treat a first job as an introduction rather than a transaction. Deliver so well that a second one is obvious, which is chapter 3's whole subject, and follow whatever the platform's own rules say about contact and about continuing work outside it. Breaking those rules to dodge a fee is a bad trade. Read the current terms on the platform itself rather than a screenshot someone posted in a group chat.

## Be findable in one place, properly

Half-finished profiles scattered across six sites lose to one finished profile in one place. Finished means the service sentence from the last lesson sits at the top, one or two pieces of proof are visible without anyone asking, what you charge or how you charge is stated where the platform allows it, and there is a way to contact you that works.

Choose the route you will work for the next month and the one place you will be findable in. Then actually finish it.

## Reading a job post before you spend an hour on it

Signs it is real and funded: a described outcome rather than a job title, such as "our weekly newsletter built and sent every Tuesday". A budget or a range. Dates. A client who answers questions when applicants ask them.

Signs to be careful: no outcome, no number anywhere, no reply to a direct question, and a description that would fit any freelancer alive.

## Three warnings that belong to the agreement

These are not about your nerves. They are about whether a workable agreement exists at all.

**You are asked to pay to start.** A training fee, an equipment deposit, a processing charge, a placement fee, refundable or otherwise. Basic Finance already holds that rule flat, that an employer pays you and you do not pay an employer whatever the fee is called, and it covers the shapes the offer arrives in. What matters here is narrower: work that charges you for the privilege of doing it is not an agreement you can scope or price, so there is nothing in it for this course to teach you to write down. A platform charging you to use it is a different thing, because it is a published cost on a fee page you can read and decide about before you sign up. A person offering you a job and asking you for money before it starts has no fee page.

**The unpaid test is the actual deliverable.** A short exercise invented for the purpose is normal. Being asked to produce the thing that ships on Friday, before anything is agreed, is not a test. Telling one from the other, and the four questions to ask when you cannot, is the resume and portfolio course's subject. What belongs here is what it means for the agreement: work that ships has a price and a date, or it is not work, and the counter is to offer a small paid first piece.

**Pressure to leave the platform before anything is agreed.** Someone who wants your details and your time moved somewhere unrecorded, urgently, before scope or payment is written down, is removing the record rather than saving a fee.

Two sibling courses take the other angles on that last one. A fake recruiter collecting your ID photos and bank details belongs to the online safety course. A buyer pushing a seller off-platform to escape payment protection belongs to the online selling course. Here it is an agreement problem, and chapter 2 is where you learn to write the agreement.

## What you can now do

Open the last two job posts you were going to apply to and mark, for each, whether an outcome, a number, a date and a poster who answers questions are actually there. Apply to the one that carries more of them, and leave the other where it is.

lessons.title: The message that gets a reply
lessons.content_mdx:
# The message that gets a reply

Picture the person reading it. They posted a job, or they opened an email they were not expecting, and they have a business to run. They are not evaluating you. They are deciding whether this message deserves more attention than the next one in the pile.

Everything below follows from that.

One boundary first. This lesson is about the message you send to a client: a proposal on a marketplace, or a cold email to a business. Applying to an employer for a job, with a CV and an application form, is a different craft and it lives in the resume and portfolio course.

## The shape

Five parts, in this order.

**Their problem, in their words.** Open on them, not on you. "You are posting every day and the captions are eating your whole morning." A client should recognise their own situation in your first line.

**What you would do about it.** One or two sentences of an actual approach, specific enough that it could turn out to be wrong. This is the part that separates you from everyone who wrote "I can help you with this."

**One piece of proof.** The most relevant sample you have, linked so it opens without anyone requesting access. One. A list of five dilutes the one that mattered.

**What they asked for.** Availability, a start date, a rate or a range if the post asked for one, and anything else the post specified.

**One question.** A real one that shows you read the post. "Are the product photos existing, or is shooting them part of this?"

Then stop. No closing paragraph about your dedication.

## What kills it

**A wall about you.** Where you studied, your work ethic, your commitment to excellence. The client has not agreed to care about you yet.

**A template carrying the last client's name.** It happens because you are sending forty of them. Eight messages that are actually read beat forty that are not.

**Every tool you have ever opened.** A list of fourteen tools tells the client you are guessing which one they wanted.

**Need used as a reason to hire you.** "I really need this job." "Please give me a chance, I am new." It is honest and it is human, and it moves the decision onto pity, where you lose to whoever talked about the client's problem instead. Your situation is real. It is not an argument.

## The buried instruction

Clients hide a small instruction inside a post to find out who read it. Start your message with the word mango. Name your favourite film. Put the word peso in the subject line.

Answer it, in the first line, with no comment about how clever the trick was. Skipping it is the cheapest way there is to be filtered out, and leading with your credentials instead does not rescue you, because the instruction was the credential being tested.

Answer everything else that was asked as well, including the boring parts. A post that asks for three things and gets two back has already told the client what working with you will be like.

## When you have no relevant sample

Do not apologise, and do not send something unrelated.

Marlon wanted a first client for email work. A wholesale supplier in Bulacan posted for someone to run their promo emails. He rewrote one of the emails sitting in their public newsletter archive, sent both versions side by side, and said what he changed and why. It took him an hour. He was the only applicant who had touched their actual material.

That is not free work. It is one deliberate piece, aimed at one buyer, that you chose to make and could have sent to nobody. It is not the same as being handed the live deliverable before anything is agreed, which is the thing the last lesson told you to refuse.

## Following up

Once.

You choose the interval, you state it in the original message, and then you keep to it. "If it is easier, I will follow up on Thursday."

A follow-up is three lines. What you sent. One new and useful thing, such as a second sample or something you noticed about their site. A clean exit: "If the timing is wrong, no problem, I will leave it here." Then leave it there. Messaging a stranger every morning costs you the client you might have had from them six months later.

## When they reply

The reply is not the job. It is a conversation in which you find out what the job actually is, and that conversation is where beginners lose money, because they agree to a price before they know what they agreed to do.

Bring questions. What exactly is being delivered, and how many. By when. What they need to give you, and when it arrives. Who decides it is finished.

That is chapter 2, and it is where the money is decided.

## What you can now do

Take a post you were going to apply to and write the five parts: their problem in their words, what you would do, one linked sample, everything the post asked for, and one real question. Delete whatever is left over, and name in the message the day you will follow up.

quiz.prompt: Danica can make basic graphics, write captions and cut short clips. She is writing the top line of her freelance profile and wants a client to be able to act on it. Which line does that?

options.text: Creative and hardworking freelancer, fast learner, open to any kind of task.
Graphics, captions, video editing, data entry and admin support, at flexible rates for new clients.
I build a month of captioned posts for small food businesses, delivered ready to schedule.
Available immediately for any creative project, any industry, short or long term, competitive rates.

quiz.explanation: A client arrives with a problem already worded in their own head, and they are looking for the sentence that answers it. Danica's third line names who it is for, what they get, and roughly the size of it, so a food seller reading it knows in one line whether to click. The other three make the client do the matching, and a client will not. The long skill list is the worst of them, because it fails twice: four services read as four half-services, and a rate is built out of a job you have done before, so an offer of anything makes every job your first job and every estimate a guess. Flexible and competitive rates say nothing except that you will go lower.

quiz.prompt: Elmer wants a sample he can show, and no client has ever paid him. He has two free days this week and no brief from anybody. What is the best use of those two days?

options.text: Rebuild something real for a business he could actually serve, and record what the situation was and what he changed.
Work free for a month for the first business that agrees to it, so that he can describe himself as experienced afterwards.
Take a short course and put the certificate up, since a sample means little until somebody has paid him for one.
Practise on invented brands until he has ten pieces, then start applying once the collection looks full enough.

quiz.explanation: You do not need a client's permission to make proof. One piece of work aimed at one real business, with the situation, what you did and what changed written beside it, is evidence about a real problem. A folder of invented brands is a practice file about nothing, and a certificate says you attended, not that you can do the work. Working free for a month is the expensive version of the same mistake: it buys one testimonial at the price of a month, and it teaches the client that your time costs nothing. Gathering your whole inventory of evidence into a browsable portfolio is the resume and portfolio course's job. Here you need one piece, aimed at one kind of buyer.

quiz.prompt: Jenny has time for one careful proposal today. Post A asks for a VA who is hardworking and flexible, states a monthly budget, and says to start immediately. It does not say what the VA would actually do. Post B asks for weekly supplier invoices logged and chased, starting next month. It names no budget, but the poster has answered two applicants' questions in the comments. Which does she write to?

options.text: Post A, because a stated budget is the one signal proving somebody has money already set aside to spend.
Post A today and Post B tomorrow, since the funded one is worth reaching before the slot is filled.
Neither today. Ask both posters for the half that is missing, and write to whichever of them answers.
Post B, because a described outcome and a poster who answers questions beat a number attached to no job.

quiz.explanation: A budget on an undescribed job tells you what somebody will spend, not what they want done, so anything you send back is a guess you can be held to. Post B gives you the outcome, which is the thing a proposal is actually written about, and a poster answering applicants in public has shown they are present and will answer you too. The missing budget on B is a question, and it is a question you can ask inside the message you were going to send anyway. Writing to both spends the hour that made the one careful proposal careful. Asking both and waiting hands your day to whoever replies first rather than to the post that is worth the work.

quiz.prompt: Ronnie gets a marketplace message about a logo job. Before scope or price has been discussed, the client asks him to move to a personal chat app, says it is easier that way, and wants to start today. No work has been done yet. What should he do?

options.text: Move over now and settle the scope there, since a client who finds the platform awkward is not the problem.
Refuse any channel but the marketplace, because a client who asks to leave it has told him what they are.
Agree the scope, the price and the payment points in writing first, then decide the channel under the rules.
Move over, but ask for the whole fee before starting, since nothing at all protects the payment on the other side.

quiz.explanation: The problem is not the app, it is the order. Once scope, price and payment points exist in writing, moving the conversation is a preference. Before they exist, moving it removes the only record of what was agreed, and the urgency about moving is the part worth reading. Settle the agreement where you are, then follow whatever the platform's own current rules say about contact and about continuing work outside it, because breaking those to dodge a fee is a bad trade. Refusing every channel outright loses clients who simply prefer chat. Asking for the whole fee up front is a bigger ask than this needs and still leaves him working from nothing written down.

quiz.prompt: Trina has spent a year on one marketplace. The jobs are steady and small, each one ends when it ends, and she has no repeat client and no referral. Her income is flat and she wants to know what to fix. What is the real problem?

options.text: Every job ended as a transaction, so a year of work has built no relationship of her own underneath it.
Her rates sit too low for that marketplace, and one large increase will filter her toward more serious buyers.
She is on the wrong marketplace, and putting her profile on two or three others would widen the pool of buyers.
She has not applied to enough posts, so a much larger number of proposals a day is the fix.

quiz.explanation: A marketplace is a sensible place to start and a weak place to stay. It owns the buyer, sets the terms, and takes its share before the money reaches you, and it can change any of that without asking you. What makes a second year different from the first is repeat work and referrals, and both of those come out of delivery, which is chapter 3. Spreading half-finished profiles across more platforms multiplies the same problem, and more proposals a day is simply more of the thing that has not been compounding. Raising a rate may well be right eventually, but that is a chapter 2 decision and it does not answer why nothing carries forward.

quiz.prompt: Elaine has half-built profiles on four freelance sites, a Facebook page with three posts on it, and a portfolio link that asks strangers to request access. She has two evenings this week. What is the best use of them?

options.text: Start a fifth profile on a newer site with less competition, and come back to the other four next month instead.
Finish one profile properly: the service sentence, proof that opens without a request, and how she charges.
Open the portfolio link to anyone who has the address, and put that link on all four of the profiles.
Post to the Facebook page every day for two weeks, and add the page link to every profile she has.

quiz.explanation: One finished profile in one place beats four half-finished ones, because a stranger who lands on any of the four is deciding from what is in front of them. Finished has a shape: the service sentence at the top, one or two pieces of proof visible without anyone asking for access, what you charge or how you charge where the platform allows it, and contact that works. Opening the portfolio link is part of that rather than the whole of it, since a working link on an empty profile still leaves the profile empty. A fifth profile multiplies the problem she already has. Daily posting fills a page nobody has a reason to visit yet.

quiz.prompt: A job post ends with a line saying to start your message with the word mango. Aldrin has strong samples and a relevant degree, and he thinks the instruction is a gimmick. How should he open the message?

options.text: Lead with his degree and experience, then work mango in near the end so it still shows he read it.
Start with mango, then their problem, then one relevant sample and the question he wants answered.
Skip it, because a serious client judges the work, and a word game is not what he would be hired for.
Put mango in the subject line only, and use the message itself for a full account of his background.

quiz.explanation: The instruction is the filter. Answering it first, with no commentary about how clever it was, costs one word and proves the only thing being tested, which is whether you read what was in front of you. Burying it at the end, or parking it in the subject line while the message itself is about you, misses twice, because a wall about yourself is the other thing that gets a message closed. Skipping it is the cheapest way there is to be sorted out of the pile, and strong samples cannot rescue a message nobody opened. The order that works is their problem, what you would do, your most relevant proof, what they asked for, and one real question.

quiz.prompt: Marlon sent a proposal on Monday and said in it that he would follow up on Thursday. It is Thursday afternoon and the client has not replied at all. What should he send?

options.text: Nothing at all. Following up reads as desperate, and a client who wants him will come back on their own.
A short note now, then another next Thursday, and one more the Thursday after if nothing comes back.
A note asking only whether the role is still open, with nothing added, so it stays short and easy to answer.
A short note: what he sent, one new and useful thing, and a clean exit if the timing is wrong for them.

quiz.explanation: He said Thursday, so Thursday is when he writes. Choosing the interval yourself and stating it up front turns a chase into a kept commitment, which is the first thing a client ever learns about how you work. The follow-up carries one new and useful thing so it is worth opening, and a clean exit so silence stays comfortable for both of you. A note with nothing new in it asks the client to do all the work of the exchange. A standing weekly cadence keeps you in an inbox you were not invited back into, and it is the exit that makes a single follow-up welcome. Saying nothing is not restraint, it is leaving a decision unmade because of a story you told yourself about how it looks.

lessons.title: Pin the work down before you quote
lessons.content_mdx:
# Pin the work down before you quote

Marilou does virtual assistant work from Iloilo. A message arrives: "Hi, how much for social media management for my milk tea shop?"

She could answer that in ten seconds. Whatever she says becomes the number she is held to, for a job neither of them has described yet. One shop wants three posts a week on one page. Another wants daily posts on three platforms, a reply to every comment, and a report at the end of the month. Same seven words, completely different jobs.

You cannot price what you have not defined. A number given before scoping is not a price. It is a guess with your name on it.

## The questions that turn a request into a countable job

Ask these before you say anything about money. On a call, in a message, in a form you send over. It does not matter which, as long as the answers come back in writing.

**What exactly is delivered, and how many?** Not "social media management". Twelve captions a month, twelve matching graphics, posted to one Facebook page.

**What does done look like?** For a caption, done is posted. For a logo, done is the files in the formats they can actually open and use. Say which formats.

**What do you need from them, and by when?** Photos, logins, product prices, the brand colours. Name the date you need each one.

**What happens to your delivery date if their material arrives late?** Decide this now, while everyone is calm and friendly. The sensible answer is usually that your date moves by however long you waited.

**How many rounds of changes are included, and what counts as a round?** One round is one consolidated set of comments, sent once. Six separate messages over four days is not one round, and if you do not write that down, it will be.

**What is not included?** This is the one that saves you.

One thing this lesson deliberately leaves alone: the formal sign-off, meaning who is allowed to approve a deliverable and on what conditions. That matters once you are running several clients at once, and the client operations course owns it.

## The exclusion list protects you more than the inclusion list

Everything you listed as delivered is a promise you made. Everything you did not list is an argument waiting to happen, because they assumed it was in there and you assumed it was not.

Dante builds websites in Davao. His scope says five pages, built on the client's existing theme, with text and photos supplied by the client. Then his exclusions say: not included are writing the text, sourcing or licensing photos, setting up the domain and hosting, uploading products, and training staff to use it.

Not one of those lines cost him anything to write. Each one is a conversation he now gets to have before he has already done the work for free.

## Size it by walking through it, not by feel

"That will take about a week" is a feeling. Write out the actual steps instead and put a time against each one.

Joan writes product descriptions in Baguio. Asked for eight of them, she does one first: read the brief, look at the item, draft, cut it back, check it against the client's tone, format it. She times herself doing exactly that, then multiplies by eight.

Then she adds the parts that always happen and never appear in anybody's estimate:

- the briefing call, and the messages before and after it
- reading the feedback and applying the changes
- the admin, meaning the quote, the invoice and the follow up

That is the real size of the job. If the number that comes out frightens you, the number was always that. You were simply not counting it.

## The first job with a new client is the loosest

You do not know yet how they give feedback, how fast they reply, or whether "make it pop" is going to arrive four separate times. They do not know yet whether you deliver at all.

So make the first piece small and paid. One landing page rather than the whole site. One month of posts rather than a six-month retainer. A small job that goes well converts into a big one on far better terms, because by then you both know the shape of the work. A big job with an unknown client is how a bad month turns into a bad quarter.

## What you can now do

Take any vague request sitting in your inbox and turn it into a written list: deliverables with counts, exclusions, revision rounds, and what the client owes you and when. That list is the thing you put a price on in the next lesson. Anything on it you cannot answer yet is a question to ask, not a reason to discount.

lessons.title: Where your number comes from
lessons.content_mdx:
# Where your number comes from

Everybody wants to be handed a rate. Nobody can hand you one honestly, because your number is built out of your costs, your hours and your obligations, and no one else carries yours.

What follows is arithmetic you can run tonight.

## Start from what you need, not from what other people charge

Angeline keeps books for small businesses in Bacolod. Her arithmetic goes like this.

**What she needs in a month.** Household, transport, food, phone and internet come to ₱26,000. Then the things a freelancer carries that a salaried bookkeeper does not. A laptop that has to be replaced eventually, a backup connection for when the main one dies, and the weeks between clients are amounts she can estimate, so she puts a figure against them and adds it in: ₱8,000 a month. Her monthly target is ₱34,000.

Her contributions and taxes do not belong in that column at all. They move with what she bills rather than with what she spends, so they are not a cost she can name in advance and add up. They sit on top of the rate as a share of every peso invoiced, not as a line in her costs.

On those contributions and taxes: a registered freelancer has filing and contribution obligations on a schedule, and the current rules, amounts and deadlines live on the BIR, SSS, PhilHealth and Pag-IBIG sites themselves. Look them up at the source rather than trusting a figure from a Facebook group, or from here.

**How many hours she can actually bill.** Angeline works five days a week. She does not bill five days a week. Briefing calls, chasing clients for bank statements, her own invoicing, the gaps between jobs: call it four billable hours a day rather than eight. That is twenty billable hours a week, roughly eighty-eight a month.

**Her floor.** ₱34,000 divided by 88 hours is a little under ₱400 an hour. Below that line she is working at a loss and calling it a business.

That is her floor before contributions and tax. Whatever share those take of what she bills goes on top of it, which is why a rate set exactly at the floor is a rate set below it. What that share is for you depends on how you are registered and what you earn, and it is published by the offices that run it. Look it up before you quote, not after.

Those figures are Angeline's, invented so the arithmetic is visible. Yours will be different. The method will not.

A floor is not a price. It is the line you now know you are standing on.

## Three shapes, and when each fits

**By the hour.** Simple, easy to explain, and it punishes you for getting good. Ryan edits podcast episodes in Quezon City. An episode used to take him five hours. It now takes two, because he built a template and learned his shortcuts. Billing by the hour, his reward for that improvement is a pay cut.

**By the deliverable.** One price for one finished thing. The client weighs it against what the thing is worth to them rather than against your speed, and every hour you save stays yours. Move to this shape as soon as you can size a job reliably.

**A monthly retainer.** For work that repeats: a set amount of output every month for a set fee. Write down what a month contains, or a retainer quietly becomes unlimited.

## Say the number, then stop talking

State it plainly. "For that scope the fee is [your number], with part of it before I start."

Then stop. Do not apologise for it. Do not add "but I can adjust". Do not offer a discount nobody asked for. The silence after a price always feels longer to the person who said it than to the person hearing it.

## When they say it is too expensive

You have three moves.

**Hold.** "I understand. That is my rate for this scope."

**Reduce the scope to fit the budget.** "With that budget I can do eight descriptions instead of twelve." The price moved because the work moved. That is honest, and the client can see the trade.

**Decline.** Some jobs are not worth doing at any number you would take, and saying so early is cheaper for both of you than discovering it in month three. Haggling itself is not the signal. A small business owner spending money they can feel will push, and pushing twice is ordinary. What is worth weighing is a client who has pushed the price twice and asked nothing at all about what the work involves, because that is a preview of how the job will run.

The move that is not on the list is dropping the price while the work stays the same. Do that once and you have taught that client what your work is worth. Every job after it starts from the lower figure.

## Raising it with an existing client

Two decisions, and both are yours. First, what the new number is: rebuild it from today's arithmetic rather than adding a bit to the old one. Second, the date it takes effect, far enough ahead that the client can plan around it. Price a brand new client at your real number straight away, because no stranger should inherit the rate you set two years ago.

How that message is worded is the client communication course's subject. The decision behind it is this one's.

## What you can now do

Work out your own monthly target, your own honest billable hours, and divide. That is your floor. Now take the scoped job from the last lesson, size it in hours, and price it as one deliverable at a figure comfortably above the floor.

lessons.title: Putting it in writing
lessons.content_mdx:
# Putting it in writing

An agreement is not really about court. It is about memory.

Six weeks from now you and your client will remember the same conversation differently, and both of you will be completely sincere. Terms in writing mean neither of you has to win that argument. You open the email instead.

## What has to exist in writing before you start

Not a fifteen-page contract. A list, agreed by both of you, that covers:

**Who the parties are.** Your name and business name, theirs, and the person you will actually be dealing with day to day.

**The deliverables and the exclusions.** Straight out of the last two lessons, with counts.

**The dates, and what the client owes you.** Their material, their approvals, their logins, each with a date against it, and what happens to your delivery date when those arrive late.

**The price, and what triggers each payment.** Not only the total. Say what has to happen before each part of it falls due.

**The revision rounds, and what a change costs.** How many are included, and the plain statement that work beyond them is quoted separately rather than absorbed.

**Who owns the finished work, and when.** Agree it out loud: ownership passes on full payment, or on delivery, or you keep it and license its use. What you must not do is leave it unsaid and assume your version.

**Confidential material.** What you will not repeat, and whether you may show the work in your portfolio. Ask about the portfolio, because "no" is a normal answer and finding out afterwards is worse.

**How either side ends it.** Notice, what is owed for work already done, and what gets handed over on the way out.

If you can only get some of this agreed before the work starts, get the money first: the deliverables, the payment triggers and the dates. Ownership and confidentiality can be settled in the same thread a day later. A missing payment trigger costs you this month. A missing ownership line costs you at handover.

## Payment terms are risk control, not rudeness

These are arrangements freelancers use. Each one is something the two of you agree and write down, not a rule that exists somewhere waiting to be quoted:

- part of the fee before work starts
- payment split across stages on a longer job, each stage tied to something visible being delivered
- final files released on final payment

Nikki illustrates children's books from Cavite. She takes part of the fee before she opens a file, and the layered artwork goes over on the balance. Nobody has ever refused her. The clients who would have refused are exactly who the arrangement exists for.

If you are already mid-job with nothing agreed, you can still raise it. Say what you have finished, propose that part of the fee is settled before you carry on, and put the rest of the terms in the same message.

## The email that counts as a record

You do not need a signature to have a record.

After the call, Marilou sends the milk tea shop this: "Hi Ma'am, confirming what we agreed: twelve captions and twelve graphics a month, posted to the Facebook page, two revision rounds included, product photos from you by the 25th of the month before, [your figure] a month with part of it up front. Please confirm this is correct."

When "Yes, correct" comes back, both of you are holding a dated record of the same job.

What is not a record: a voice call nobody wrote up, a promise buried in a chat thread neither of you can find three months later, and "but we discussed it".

## When the client sends their own contract

Read all of it, including the pages after the signature block. Then:

- Ask about anything you do not understand. "What does this clause mean in practice?" is a normal professional question, and a client who is irritated by it has told you something useful.
- Never sign a scope you have not seen. If the contract refers to an annex, a brief or a statement of work, read that document too.
- Watch for open-ended terms: unlimited revisions, work owned before payment, no way for you to end it.
- Ask for a change where you need one. A contract someone sends you is an opening position, not a verdict.

## Where this lesson stops

This is not legal advice, and this course cannot give any. Whether an agreement needs notarising, whether an emailed confirmation binds anybody, and what routes exist if it all goes wrong are questions for a lawyer, and the requirements change over time. When a job is large enough that the answer matters, pay for an hour of a lawyer's time. It costs less than the job does.

## What you can now do

Write the confirmation email for a job you are about to start: deliverables, exclusions, dates, price and payment triggers, revision rounds, ownership, and how either side ends it. Send it, and get "yes, correct" back before you begin.

quiz.prompt: A message reaches Cherry, who keeps books for small shops: "Hi, how much to handle our books?" She has never spoken to this person before. What should she send back?

options.text: Questions first: how many accounts, how many transactions a month, who supplies the records, and what they need.
Her usual monthly figure right away, because a fast reply shows she is responsive and the details can follow after.
A deliberately low figure to secure the shop ahead of anyone else, then a higher one once she sees the work.
A very wide range now, with a note that the real figure depends on details she will collect from them later on.

quiz.explanation: Those six words could describe one shop with a shoebox of receipts, or three outlets with staff payouts and a supplier ledger behind them. A figure sent before the job is described is a guess she will be held to. A wide range is the same guess with more room to be dragged downward, and an opening low figure teaches the client what the work is worth before she has learned anything about it. Questions cost her nothing and are what a professional sounds like.

quiz.prompt: Ferdie agreed to build a four-part onboarding email sequence for a training centre, delivered in three weeks. The written scope named the four emails and the fee and nothing else. The centre sent its course details in week three and is now on the fourth round of changes. What was missing from that scope?

options.text: A larger fee at the start, and a charge for every week the project runs on past the agreed three weeks.
A clause letting him leave the project, and a limit on how long a round of feedback can run for.
A line making the three weeks an estimate, and a note that dates move whenever the work grows.
A revision-round limit, a date for the centre's material, and what a late handover does to the date.

quiz.explanation: Both problems come from one omission: the scope described what Ferdie owed and never described what the centre owed. A revision-round limit caps the changes, a date for the material makes the delay visible, and a line moving the delivery date when the handover is late means the slipped deadline is not silently his fault. A bigger fee with a weekly late charge covers this job and no other, and it prices a delay rather than preventing it. An exit clause and a feedback window are both real terms, and neither of them tells the centre when its own material is due. Calling the date an estimate protects nobody and tells the client that dates here do not mean much.

quiz.prompt: Sheryl is asked to design six social media templates for a gym. She has built one before, for a friend, and has no real idea what six of them takes. How should she size the job?

options.text: Copy the figure a friend charged for a similar set of templates, since that friend has already done the work.
Build one template end to end, time herself doing it, multiply by six, then add briefing, revisions and admin.
Add a large safety margin on top of a rough guess, so that an overrun cannot hurt her whatever the job becomes.
Quote by the hour instead, so that however long the job turns out to take, the clock keeps her covered for it.

quiz.explanation: Sizing means walking through the work, not feeling your way around it. Timing one real unit gives Sheryl a number she can defend, and the briefing, revisions and admin are the parts that always happen and never make it into an estimate. Her friend's figure came out of her friend's speed and situation. A padded guess is still a guess, and it is usually padded in the wrong place. Hourly does not size the job at all, it just moves the surprise onto the invoice.

quiz.prompt: Lito builds monthly report decks for a property agency and bills by the hour. He built a template, and the deck that used to take him six hours now takes two. His income has dropped. What should he change?

options.text: Nothing. Bill the two hours and accept the drop, since a client paying by the hour is only paying for time worked.
Keep billing hourly, and quote a minimum number of hours per deck so a fast month cannot fall below what it is worth.
Move to a price per finished deck, set at a figure he is happy with, so that the speed he earned belongs to him.
Keep billing hourly and raise his rate each time he gets faster, so that the total per deck stays where it was.

quiz.explanation: Hourly billing charges for time, so getting better at the work cuts your pay. A price per deck is weighed against what a finished deck is worth to the agency rather than against Lito's speed, and every hour he saves after that is his. A minimum-hours floor is hourly billing arguing with itself, and the first thing the agency will ask is what the minimum is for. Ratcheting the hourly rate to hold the same total is a deliverable price wearing a disguise, and it forces an awkward conversation every few months instead of one clean change now. Accepting the drop means the days he spent building the template were a pay cut he paid for himself.

quiz.prompt: Grace quoted a monthly figure to keep a small restaurant's books. The owner replies that it is too expensive. Grace built that figure from her own costs and billable hours and is comfortable with it. What are her real options?

options.text: Hold the figure, or offer a smaller version of the job that fits the budget he has, or decline the work politely.
Cut the figure by a fifth while keeping the same monthly work, so the owner can see she is willing to be reasonable.
Explain why the rate is fair and how much experience sits behind it, then repeat the same figure to him.
Take the lower figure for three months as a trial, then move him up to the full rate once he sees the value.

quiz.explanation: Price and scope move together, or neither moves. Holding, shrinking the job to fit the money, and declining are all honest positions. Cutting the fee while the work stays the same teaches the client what her work is worth, and every later job starts from the lower number. The trial rate is that same discount with a date on it, and the conversation about ending it is harder than the one she is avoiding now. Justifying the rate at length reads as nerves and invites more pushing.

quiz.prompt: Karen agreed a logo and packaging job over the phone with Tita Baby, a family friend who runs a bakery in Bulacan. The scope, the fee and the deadline were all discussed on the call. Tita Baby says there is no need for papers between family. What should Karen do before starting?

options.text: Ask her to sign a formal contract before starting, since a job taken on without one is not worth the risk to her.
Send a short email setting out what was agreed and ask Tita Baby to reply confirming that it is correct.
Write up her own detailed notes of the call and keep them safely, in case there is a disagreement later on.
Start the work and raise the terms in writing later, once there is something finished to point at.

quiz.explanation: Writing it down is about shared memory, not a courtroom. A confirmation email that gets a "yes, correct" back is a dated record both of them hold, and it costs nothing socially because it reads as being organised rather than as being suspicious. Karen's private notes record only her version, which is exactly the thing in dispute. Terms produced after the work has started are the hardest to agree. Demanding a signed contract from a family friend is likely to sour the job it was meant to protect.

quiz.prompt: An agency sends Miguel a six-page contract for video editing work. One clause gives the agency ownership of all materials produced, which he does not fully understand, and another line mentions revisions until the client is satisfied. What is the professional move?

options.text: Sign it, because an established agency with a proper contract department is unlikely to ever use it against a freelancer.
Sign it now to keep the job, and note privately which clauses he will push back on with the next client instead.
Take it to a lawyer before replying at all, since one clause is about ownership and he does not fully understand it.
Reply asking what those two clauses would mean in practice, and propose wording for both that he is comfortable with.

quiz.explanation: A contract someone sends you is an opening position, not a verdict. Asking what a clause means in practice is a normal question, and proposing wording shows he read it and still wants the job. Revisions until satisfied is an open-ended promise no fee can cover, so it has to be pinned down now. Signing something he does not understand hands the agency both the argument and his working files, and noting it for the next client leaves this one unfixed. Paid legal advice is the right move when a job is large enough that the answer matters, and it is worth knowing that. On an editing contract it spends money and a week on a question the agency will answer in a reply.

quiz.prompt: Belen agreed a fee for a set of wedding invitation designs. Nothing was said about payment timing, and she has now finished roughly half the drafts. She has no money in hand and no written terms. What should she do?

options.text: Finish everything and send the full set over first, then ask for payment, because raising money halfway through looks distrustful.
Stop work straight away and tell the client that nothing further will be sent until the whole fee has been settled in full.
Message now proposing that part of the fee is settled before she continues, and confirm the remaining terms in the same message.
Carry on as agreed and simply ask for money up front from her next client, treating this job as a lesson learned.

quiz.explanation: Payment terms are an arrangement, so they can still be proposed mid-job, and the moment she has finished work to point at is the moment she has the most standing to raise it. Folding the rest of the terms into the same message closes the whole gap at once. Delivering everything first leaves her holding all of the risk. Demanding the full fee before any delivery is a bigger ask than she needs and invites a fight. Saying nothing means this job runs on hope right to the end.
