modules.description: The agreement only matters if you run the job against it. Deliver so nobody has to ask, invoice so it can be paid, and know the proportionate move when the work keeps growing, the client goes quiet, or it is time to end.

lessons.title: Delivering what you promised
lessons.content_mdx:
# Delivering what you promised

A client hires you a second time for reasons that have little to do with talent. They hire you again because the first job cost them no attention. They knew what was coming, it arrived when you said it would, and it was usable the moment they opened it.

Reliability is also the only real defence you have when a client is unhappy. If you can point at what was agreed, what you sent and when you sent it, a disagreement stays a disagreement about the work. Without that record it becomes your word against theirs, and the person holding the money wins that one.

## Start the job on purpose

The first hour of a job decides how the rest of it goes.

Confirm the scope in writing, in the words you settled in chapter 2: what you are delivering, what you are not, how many rounds of changes are included, and the dates. Confirm what the client owes you and when, because a job cannot start on the promise of files.

Then collect the inputs before you begin. Brand files, logins, the actual copy, the product samples, the name of the person who approves the work. If half of it is missing, say so on day one and say what the missing half does to the date. A deadline you accepted while still waiting for a file is a deadline you agreed to miss.

Then tell the client what you will send and when. One line is enough. A short progress note at a point you both agreed removes the anxious check-ins before they start, and how to word that note belongs to the client communication course rather than to this one.

## Hand over so it can be used

Sending a file is not the same as handing over work.

Rowena edits product photos for a bag seller in Cebu. On her first job she sent forty files still named by her camera. The client spent an evening working out which was which, then asked for the whole set again, renamed. That evening was free work Rowena did twice.

Send the agreed format. Name the files so that a stranger opening the folder can tell what each one is. Put them somewhere the client can reach without requesting access. Add a short note: what is included, what changed since the last version, and what the client does next.

If the work needs something from the client, say what it is. Not "let me know."

## When you are going to miss a date

Say so before the date, not after it.

Marvin writes a monthly newsletter for a dental clinic in Marikina. One Wednesday he could see that Friday was gone. He wrote that morning: the draft would land Sunday, the reason was one sentence, and he gave the reason once. The clinic moved its send. Nothing else happened.

The version that ends relationships is silence until Monday, after the client has spent Friday afternoon and a whole weekend wondering. A missed date is a scheduling problem. A missed date the client discovered on their own is a trust problem, and better work later does not repair it.

Give a new date you can actually hit, then hit it. Missing once is normal.

A second miss on the same job is different in kind, because the client has stopped weighing a date and started weighing whether any date from you is real. A third date from the same source does not answer that. What does is shrinking the promise. Cut the next delivery down to a piece you can certainly hand over, send it on the day you said, and agree the remainder as its own commitment with its own date. One small kept promise restores more than one large hopeful one. Then look at whether you have taken on more than you can carry, because two misses on one job is usually an answer to that question rather than a run of bad luck.

## Feedback, and work that comes back

Some of what you send comes back. Read it once, then sort it before you reply.

There are two piles. In the first, the client is saying the work does not match what was agreed: wrong size, a missing item, a fact that is wrong, a file that will not open. That is yours to fix, inside the revision rounds, without argument and without a defence of your process.

In the second, the client is asking for something different from what was agreed. New pages, a new direction, a fifth version after two rounds. That is not feedback. That is a change, and the last lesson of this chapter is about what to do with it.

Sorting a message into those two piles before you answer is what keeps you from arguing about a genuine mistake, or from absorbing a new project for nothing.

## Keep your own record

One place, updated as you go: what was agreed, what you sent, the date you sent it, and what the client approved.

A folder and a running note are enough when you have one or two clients. Running several clients at once needs a system, and that system is the client operations course.

You will reach for this record twice. Once when somebody asks what happened six weeks ago, and once when an invoice has not been paid and the record is the thing that makes that conversation short.

## What you can now do

For the job you are running now, write the four lines: what was agreed, what you have sent, the date you sent it, what they approved. Put them somewhere you will find them again, because that is the file you will reach for twice.

lessons.title: Sending the invoice and getting paid
lessons.content_mdx:
# Sending the invoice and getting paid

Delivering and being paid are two separate events, and the gap between them is where new freelancers lose money quietly. The work went out, the client said thank you, and then nothing was ever billed, or it was billed to somebody whose job is not paying anybody.

## What makes an invoice payable

An invoice is not a request for a favour. It is a document the client's finance side can act on without asking you a question first, which means three things have to be true of it. It carries a number both of you can refer to later, rather than "the invoice". It describes the work in the same words as the agreement, so it can be matched against what was approved. And it names the due date you agreed and exactly how to pay you, account details and payment reference included. Anything the payer has to email you about is a delay you built yourself.

The full anatomy of an invoice, what a receipt is as against the document a registered seller has to issue, and how to run a numbering sequence that never collides are the bookkeeping course's subject. What this lesson owes you is the part that is about the client rather than about the paperwork, which is who you send it to and what you do when it is not paid.

## Send it to the person who pays

The person who briefed you may not be the person who pays you.

Joy edits podcast audio for a small firm in Ortigas. Her first invoice sat with the marketing officer who hired her for three weeks. There was no malice in it. Paying suppliers simply was not that person's job, and nobody told her it had arrived.

Ask at the start, while everyone is friendly: who should the invoice go to, and what do they need on it? Some clients want a reference number of their own. Some need it before a particular day to make that month's payment run. Ask once, write down the answer, and the next twelve invoices are easy.

Then invoice on the schedule you agreed rather than when you happen to remember. If the agreement says part on signing, part at the halfway point and the balance on delivery, send each one on the day it falls due.

## The ladder

Late payment gets a rising, unemotional response. Every rung is dated and specific, and every rung assumes the last one simply was not seen.

1. Near the due date, a short reminder: invoice number, amount, due date, payment details again.
2. After the due date, a firmer note with the invoice attached again, stating that it is now overdue and asking for a payment date.
3. Then a message that names the consequence, such as further work pausing on a stated date until the invoice is settled. Only write this if you agreed it and intend to do it.
4. Then a decision, which is not a message at all: does this client get any more of your time?

Every rung stays calm. One angry message feels excellent for about a minute, ends the relationship without producing money, and hands the client something to talk about instead of their bill. The sentences for each rung are the client communication course's subject. The decision behind them is yours.

If you agreed that work pauses when payment stops, pause. A term you never enforce is a term you do not have.

## Keep the money record

Two columns will do at the start: what you invoiced, and what actually arrived. Invoice number, client, amount, date sent, date paid.

That record answers the one question you cannot answer from memory, which is who owes you what today. It is also what you hand to anybody helping you sort out a real dispute later.

## What this lesson will not tell you

Registration, the documents a registered seller has to issue, and tax obligations all exist for freelancers here, and what applies to you depends on how you are registered and what you earn. These rules change.

So this lesson names none of them. No form numbers, no thresholds, no rates, no filing dates. Whatever a course, a Facebook group or a chatbot tells you about those is worth nothing next to the BIR's own site, and the same holds for business name registration with DTI and for SSS, PhilHealth and Pag-IBIG. Look them up at the source, on the day you need them.

The same rule covers the rails your money travels on. Fees, transfer times and limits for banks, e-wallets and remittance services all change, so check the provider's current schedule yourself before you promise a client anything about how payment will arrive.

## What you can now do

Write the invoice for the job you are on now. Before you send it, ask the client two things: who it should go to, and what they need on it. Then put the invoice number, the amount and the date you sent it into your money record on the same day, and leave the paid column empty until it is not.

lessons.title: Scope creep, silence, and the exit
lessons.content_mdx:
# Scope creep, silence, and the exit

Three things end freelance jobs badly. The work quietly grows, the client goes quiet, or the relationship reaches its end and nobody handles the ending. Each one has a proportionate move, and none of the moves is a feeling.

## The work that grows

Scope creep never arrives as a demand. It arrives as "while you're at it" and "quick lang." Each request is small, each one is easy to say yes to, and the fifth one is a project you are doing for free.

The answer is not refusing and it is not absorbing. It is naming.

Rowena agreed twelve edited photos with two rounds of changes. After the second round the client asked for four more shots, a different crop for a banner, and a version with the price laid over it. Her reply did three things. It named what sat outside the agreed twelve, it gave a price for that extra work, and it gave a date the extra work would be ready. The client took two of the three items and dropped the other. Nobody was insulted.

The reference point is the scope you wrote in chapter 2, not your patience. That is what the exclusions list was for. Without it you are arguing about memory, and memory arguments go to whoever sounds more certain.

When a client says it was always included, do not call them a liar and do not fold. Quote the line from the agreement, say what you understood the job to be, and offer the extra as priced work with a date. If the agreement turns out to be genuinely vague, that is a lesson about your next scope, and the cheapest ending is often to do the small thing once and tighten the wording before the next job.

Writing those sentences well is the client communication course's subject. Tracking changes across several clients at once is the client operations course's. What belongs here is the money: a change has a price and a date, or it is not a change, it is a gift.

## The client who goes quiet

There is a real difference between a busy client and a stalled one. A busy client answers late and still moves the work forward. A stalled client has stopped, and your job is sitting in the middle of their silence with your hours already spent.

Decide a follow up cadence and say it out loud instead of messaging daily. Something like: a note now, another in a few days, and if there is still nothing after that, the work pauses and you will pick it back up when they are ready. Then do exactly that.

Where you stop matters. Get the work to a clean point, write down what is finished and what is waiting on them, and send that as a dated note. It protects you twice. The client cannot later say nothing was delivered, and you can restart without reconstructing where you were.

This is what the up front payment and the paused work term were written for. If part of the fee arrived before you started, a stalled client costs you time but not the whole job. If nothing arrived, you have just learned why that arrangement exists, and you write it into the next agreement.

A client who goes quiet after delivery but before paying is a different case. That is not a stall. That is a late invoice, and it goes up the ladder from the previous lesson.

## Ending it

Some clients cost more than they pay. Late every time, three chases per invoice, a new emergency every weekend, a scope that moves the moment you look away. You do not have to fire anybody dramatically. You have to stop taking new work from them.

The clean version is short and forward looking. You are not able to take on new work from a stated date, you will finish what is already committed, and you wish them well. No list of grievances. A client you end well still refers people to you. A client you end badly talks about you in the same groups where your next job is sitting.

You will also be ended sometimes, for reasons that have nothing to do with you. Budgets get cut and staff change. When it happens, deliver what is committed, invoice what is owed, and ask for two things while the goodwill is still warm: a short testimonial, and permission to show the work in your portfolio.

If a client genuinely does not pay, keep your records, understand that formal routes exist, and get advice from somebody qualified before you use one. Nothing in this course is legal advice. A freelancer with a downloaded demand letter and no advice is not a plan.

## What actually keeps you in business

The freelancer who lasts is not the one who never meets a bad client. Everybody meets them.

It is the one whose scope was written down, whose invoices went out on the agreed day, and whose record of what was sent survives the argument. That is the whole difference between a bad client being survivable and a bad client being expensive.

## What you can now do

Name the client you have been absorbing changes for. Write out their next request as a change with a price and a date against it, and send that instead of doing it.

quiz.prompt: Vilma owes a restaurant its month of captions on the 28th. On the 25th she can already see that the 28th will not happen. What should she do?

options.text: Work through the weekend and send them on the 30th with a long apology attached.
Send half the captions on the 28th so that the agreed date is technically met.
Tell the restaurant on the 25th that the 30th is the new date, and say why once.
Say nothing yet, because a two day slip might still close up on its own.

quiz.explanation: A missed date is a scheduling problem. A missed date the client finds out about on their own is a trust problem, and better work later does not repair it. Telling the restaurant on the 25th lets them plan their own month around it, which is the thing they actually need. Sending half on the day buys the date and spends the credibility of every delivery after it, and waiting to see whether the slip closes up only shortens the warning the client gets.

quiz.prompt: Bea writes eight product descriptions for a hardware supplier, with one round of changes agreed. The round has been used. The client now asks for two more descriptions and a shorter version of each for the shop sign. What should she do?

options.text: Do the two extra descriptions now and charge only for the sign versions, since two more is a small ask.
Refuse both and point at the agreement, since the one round of changes was used up already.
Do all of it now and raise her price for this client the next time they book anything.
Quote both of them as a change, with a price and a date, set against the eight that were agreed.

quiz.explanation: Naming the request as a change is the move that is neither refusing nor absorbing. It uses the scope as the reference point instead of your patience, and it leaves the client a real choice: pay for both, or drop one. Splitting them, doing the descriptions free and charging only for the sign versions, prices half the change and teaches the client where the free half is. Absorbing all of it teaches them the agreed eight meant nothing, and a flat refusal spends goodwill you did not have to spend. Raising the price silently next time punishes them for something they were never told about.

quiz.prompt: Ester sent her invoice to Bernard, the operations lead who briefed the job. Three weeks later nothing has been paid and Bernard has not mentioned it at all. What should she do next?

options.text: Follow up with Bernard and ask him to walk it over to whoever pays suppliers.
Ask Bernard who processes payments, send the invoice there, and keep him copied in.
Wait another two weeks before chasing, since three weeks is not unusual for a small firm.
Assume finance will find it eventually and start the next piece for the firm.

quiz.explanation: An invoice sitting with the person who briefed you is not necessarily malice. Paying suppliers is simply not their job. Routing it to the payer while keeping your contact copied fixes this invoice and tells you who to bill next time, which is a question worth asking at the start of any engagement. Asking Bernard to walk it over keeps the invoice moving through the one person who has already not moved it, and it costs another week to find that out. Waiting longer may well match how the firm pays, and you will still be waiting without knowing who is holding it. Starting more work grows the amount you are owed.

quiz.prompt: An invoice is two weeks past the due date you both agreed. You sent one short reminder near the due date and have heard nothing back since. What is the next move?

options.text: Phone the client instead, since a conversation moves faster than another email will.
Attach the invoice again, say it is now overdue, and ask them for a payment date.
Offer to cut the amount if they settle this week, since some money beats none at all.
Send the same reminder again unchanged, in case the first one was simply missed.

quiz.explanation: The chase works as a ladder, and each rung is calm, dated and specific. Rung two attaches the invoice again, states plainly that it is overdue, and asks for a date, which gives the client one thing to answer and gives you a commitment you can quote back at rung three. A phone call can help and nothing said on it is dated or attached to the invoice, so you would be writing it down afterwards anyway. Repeating the same reminder word for word treats the second message as the first and hands the client nothing new to act on. Discounting teaches the client that waiting is profitable, and it is a rung you cannot climb back down from.

quiz.prompt: Aiza took part of her fee up front and has delivered half the work. The client has not answered for ten days, and two follow ups have gone unanswered. What should she do?

options.text: Pause at a clean point and send her a dated note on what is done and outstanding.
Finish the rest of the work anyway and invoice the balance once she is done.
Keep working on the parts that need nothing from the client, and invoice for those.
Send the finished half now so the client has something in hand while they decide.

quiz.explanation: A stalled client is not a reason to keep spending hours, and it is not a reason to disappear either. Stopping at a clean point caps what you have at risk, and the dated note gives you a record that the work was delivered and that the delay sits on their side. Finishing everything grows your exposure to a client who may not come back. Carrying on with the parts that need nothing from them is the same exposure with a better excuse, and invoicing for pieces nobody agreed to split out invites an argument about what the job even was. Sending the finished half without the note leaves work delivered and nothing written down about where it stopped.

quiz.prompt: A client insists a second landing page was always part of the deal. Your written scope lists one page, and it names the second page in the exclusions. What do you do?

options.text: Give in this once, since arguing about one page costs more than building it.
Offer to build it at half price, since the two of you plainly read the scope differently.
Build it now and add the charge to the final invoice without raising it first.
Quote the line from the scope and offer that page as priced work with a date.

quiz.explanation: The exclusions list exists for exactly this moment, and quoting it is not an accusation. It moves the conversation from whose memory is better to what was written, then gives the client a way forward that costs them money rather than costing you a weekend. Splitting the difference at half price is generous, and it concedes that a written scope is negotiable, which is the one thing you were relying on it not to be. Building it silently and billing later produces an invoice dispute at the worst possible moment, which is when you want to be paid.

quiz.prompt: A client always pays, but never before the third chase. He has just offered you another project on exactly the same terms as the last one. What do you do?

options.text: Take it on the same terms, since a client who pays late still beats no work.
Decline and tell him plainly that his payment record is the reason you refuse.
Take it only if part of the fee comes up front and payment dates are written.
Take it and quietly raise the price to cover the hours you spend chasing him.

quiz.explanation: A client who pays late is not automatically a client to drop, but repeating the arrangement that produced three chases guarantees three more. Changing the terms is the proportionate move: money up front, dated payment points, and a pause you have said you will use. Accepting the old terms keeps the cost, a blunt refusal burns a referral you could have kept, and a silent markup hides your reasoning from the one person who could fix the behaviour.

quiz.prompt: Rico has finished a set of social media graphics for a coffee shop in Davao and is about to send them across to the owner. What does handing over properly look like?

options.text: Send the agreed format, clearly named, with a short note on what is included.
Share his working folder so the client can pick whatever they want out of it.
Send the files and offer to walk the owner through them on a call this week.
Send them in his own format and convert it later if the client asks him to.

quiz.explanation: Handing over means the client can use the work without doing any of yours. Agreed format, names a stranger can read, and a short note on what is included and what happens next is the whole habit, and it is what stops a second unpaid evening of renaming and re-exporting. A walkthrough call is a good thing to offer and a poor substitute for it, because the folder still has to make sense the week after the call. A working folder pushes the sorting onto the client, and your own format means a conversion round nobody budgeted for.

questions.prompt: Nine months on a freelance marketplace. You have finished eleven small jobs, every one of them for a different buyer, and your income has not moved. You want the next nine months to look different. What actually changes it?

options.text: Go back to the eleven buyers whose work you finished, ask about repeat work and referrals, and build the relationship the marketplace was only a doorway to.
Apply to more posts every day from a saved template, since the number of applications you send is the only lever a marketplace really hands you.
Sign up on two more marketplaces so the same profile is working in three places at once, which puts your name in front of far more buyers.
Price yourself under the other applicants for a while, so that a buyer sitting there comparing you against four other people has one obvious reason to pick you.

questions.explanation: A marketplace is the easiest place to start and the weakest place to build, because the buyer is the platform's relationship and not yours. Eleven finished jobs is eleven people who have already paid you and already know your work, which is the cheapest lead you will ever have, and nobody asked them. More applications and more platforms is doing the same weak thing in more places. Pricing under everybody teaches buyers what your work is worth and leaves you no room when the volume finally arrives.

questions.prompt: Your application said you could start that day and have the whole thing finished in three days. You wrote that before you had seen the brief. The client hires you, and the brief that arrives is roughly twice the job you had pictured. What do you do?

options.text: Before you start, write to say what the three days was based on, what the brief actually contains, and the date and price the real job needs. Ask them to confirm.
Take the extra hours out of your evenings and hit the three days anyway, because the date came out of your own mouth and missing the first one you ever gave would end this.
Begin now and raise the size of the job on the third day, when the delivery is visibly not going to land and both of you can see the gap for yourselves.
Ask for more money to cover the extra work but keep the three days as promised, since the date is what won you the job and they planned their week on it.

questions.explanation: A number given before scoping is a guess you will be held to, and the moment to correct it is before any work exists, when it is still a scoping conversation rather than an excuse. Say what the estimate assumed, what the brief turned out to contain, and what the real job needs. Working nights to protect a bad estimate hides the problem and prices your next quote off the same wrong basis. Raising it on the third day is the same message delivered when the client can no longer plan around it. Charging more for a job you have not resized is agreeing to fail on time for a slightly better fee.

questions.prompt: A client you worked for once comes back with 'same as last time, same price'. Last time was agreed across a chat thread over about a week, and nothing was ever written down in one place. What do you do first?

options.text: Write out what you think 'same as last time' means as a list of deliverables and exclusions, send it over, and ask them to confirm it before you quote anything.
Quote the figure you charged before, since they were happy with the work and reopening the price is the quickest way to lose a client who came back on their own.
Quote the old figure with a quiet margin on top, because a repeat job always grows a little and the margin covers that without you having a conversation about it.
Ask for part of the fee up front this time, since the first job went through fine and a deposit is the one piece of protection you did not have on it.

questions.explanation: You cannot repeat a job neither of you can point at. 'Same as last time' is two different memories of a chat thread, and the second job is where they quietly diverge. Writing the list is quick, it costs the client nothing to confirm, and it turns an unscoped repeat into something you can price and later defend. The price is not the first question here. A margin added silently is a guess about growth you have not defined, and it leaves you arguing about a number rather than about the work. A deposit is worth agreeing too, but a deposit against an undefined job still leaves you delivering something they can call wrong.

questions.prompt: Marites quoted her last three jobs at an hourly figure she was happy with, and every one came out worse than she expected. Going back through her calendar, the briefing calls, the revision rounds and the chasing were about as much time as the work itself, and none of it was billed. What should she change?

options.text: Put the briefing calls and the chasing on the invoice at the same hourly figure, so the hours that were disappearing on her are finally being paid for.
Raise the hourly figure until those three jobs would have come out roughly where she wanted them, and then quote that new figure on everything she takes on from now on, old clients included.
Price the deliverable instead, sized by walking through every step including briefing, revisions and admin, so the parts nobody pays for by the hour sit inside the number.
Get faster at the work itself, since the billed hours are the part she controls and every hour she saves on them goes straight into what she keeps.

questions.explanation: Size a job by walking through it rather than by feel, and the walk has to include the invisible parts, because briefing, revisions and chasing happen on every job and are exactly what an hourly quote leaves outside. A deliverable price carries them without asking the client to agree that a phone call is billable, which a client has every reason to resist. Raising the hourly figure keeps the same hole and just makes it more expensive per hour, so a job with heavy revisions still loses. Getting faster actively punishes her under hourly pricing, which is the argument against it. Bill the clock and you are paid for slowness.

questions.prompt: Your written agreement says the client sends the product photos by the fifth and you deliver by the fifteenth. It is the ninth, no photos have arrived, and the client has said nothing about them. What do you do?

options.text: Hold the fifteenth and build everything you can around placeholders, then drop the real photos into the finished layouts whenever the client eventually turns them up.
Write today, say the photos are four days late, and state the new delivery date that the agreement's own terms produce. Ask them to confirm the new date.
Wait a little longer. Chasing a client for their own material looks anxious, and the fifteenth is still far enough out for the photos to arrive in time.
Deliver on the fifteenth with whatever you have been given, invoice the full amount as agreed, and treat the missing photos as the client's problem rather than yours.

questions.explanation: The reason you write down what the client owes you and by when is so that a late input has a stated consequence instead of an argument. Use it while there is still time to plan around it. Placeholders mean you do the layout twice and the second pass lands after the deadline anyway. Waiting turns their slip into your missed date, since the client will remember the fifteenth and not the fifth. Delivering something incomplete and invoicing in full is how a scope dispute starts, and you will be arguing about it from the weaker position of having already sent the work.

questions.prompt: Three weeks after you delivered, a client writes that they never received the final version and that this is why the invoice is unpaid. You did send it, to the address they gave you, on the day you said you would. What do you do?

options.text: Resend the files straight away and apologise for all of the confusion, since arguing about who sent what to whom is never worth the goodwill that it burns on the way through.
Resend it only once the invoice is settled, since the terms you agreed put final files on final payment, and a copy of the work already went across to them once.
Ask them to check with whoever briefed the job, because the work was sent as agreed and the loss almost certainly happened somewhere on their side of it.
Resend it, with the date of the original delivery and the note that went with it, because a dated record of what you sent settles this in a single message.

questions.explanation: Keeping your own record of what was sent and when is not paperwork, it is the thing that turns a payment stall into a five minute conversation. Resend and date it in the same breath, without accusation, and the invoice is back on the table. A bare apology concedes a fact that is not true and invites the same delay next time. Final files on final payment is a real term and it governs the first release, not a second copy of something already delivered, so holding this one back hands them the argument they were looking for. Telling them to go and look on their own side puts the burden on the person you want to pay you, and it does not produce the file.

questions.prompt: A client is refusing the final payment on the grounds that the work is not what was discussed. There is no written scope. There is a long chat thread, and the thread does contain their original request. What is the first move?

options.text: Tell them you will be taking this further unless the invoice is settled by the end of this week, because a firm position taken early is what moves a client who has already decided to stall.
Go back through the thread, then send one email setting out what you understood the job to be and what you delivered, and ask them to confirm it or say exactly what is missing.
Offer to redo the work at no charge, since a second pass costs you less than an unpaid invoice does and it keeps a working relationship alive out of it.
Take whatever partial amount they are willing to offer and move on, treating the shortfall as what the lesson about working without a written scope cost you.

questions.explanation: The chat thread is the only record either of you has, so the first move is to turn it into one written statement of the job and put it in front of them. Either they confirm it, which gives you the scope you never had, or they name what is missing, which gives you something specific to answer instead of a feeling. Threatening to escalate before you have established what was agreed spends the relationship and produces nothing, and what any formal route would actually involve is a question for a lawyer rather than for you in the moment. Redoing it free rewards the vagueness. Accepting a partial payment in silence settles the invoice and teaches you nothing you can use on the next client.

questions.prompt: You sent the invoice on the agreed date, a short reminder when it fell due, then a firmer one with the invoice attached again. The client replied "sorry, will process next week". Next week has been and gone and nothing has arrived. Your written terms say further work pauses if an invoice goes unsettled. What does your next message do?

options.text: Restates the amount and the original due date, and asks once more for a payment date, since the last note may simply not have been read.
Says nothing more. You have chased three times, and a fourth message only makes staying silent cheaper and easier for them to keep doing.
Names the date they gave you, states that further work is now paused until the invoice is settled, and gives the date that pause starts.
Offers to split the invoice in two so they can settle part of it now and the balance at the end of the month, which is money actually moving.

questions.explanation: Each rung of the ladder does something the last one did not, and this rung names a consequence you can actually carry out, which is only true because you agreed it in writing before the work started. Quote their own commitment back, say what happens next, and put a date on it, because a consequence with no date is a mood. Asking again for a payment date is rung two, and you have already had a date from them and watched it pass, so repeating it tells them the ladder has no rungs left. Splitting the invoice rewrites the terms in their favour immediately after a broken promise, which is the moment you have least reason to. Going silent hands them the outcome they were already drifting towards, and a term you never enforce is a term you do not have.

questions.prompt: Someone posts in a Facebook group for local business owners asking for help with an online store that has gone slow. Twenty comments underneath already say 'PM sent' and 'interested po'. You can genuinely do the work. What gets you picked?

options.text: A public reply naming the first thing you would check and why, with one link to something close to it you have done, then a short message.
A message sent before anybody else gets there, since the first name in the inbox is the one a busy poster actually opens and reads.
A comment offering to do the first fix at no charge, so they can see what your work is like before deciding to spend anything at all.
A comment listing every platform and tool you have ever worked with, so that whatever their store happens to run on, they can see you cover it.

questions.explanation: Twenty identical comments have told the poster nothing except that twenty people want work. One sentence of diagnosis says you understood the problem, and one relevant sample proves it, and both are visible to everyone else reading the thread rather than buried in a private message. Speed only wins against people doing the same thing you are. Free work here is the actual deliverable, which is the arrangement to refuse. A list of every tool you have touched reads as nobody's specialist and gives the poster nothing to act on.

questions.prompt: You have no paying clients yet. Two things are on the table. A page with a large following wants free graphics for a month, credited to you. A bakery down the road will pay a modest amount to fix one thing that is costing them orders. Which do you take?

options.text: The page. A month of visible work in front of a large audience is the fastest route to being found by the kind of people who can afford to pay you.
Both. The page builds the audience while the bakery brings in money, and at this stage you cannot really afford to turn any work away at all.
The bakery. A paid piece with a before and after gives you a client who can refer you and proof that something actually changed for a business.
Neither yet. Keep applying until a paid job at your full rate turns up, because early cheap work sets the price you will be stuck charging later.

questions.explanation: Proof is an artefact plus what the situation was, what you did and what changed. The bakery gives you all four and a person who can be asked for a referral. The page gives you a credit line and an audience that is not buying anything, and a month of unpaid deliverables is the arrangement to be careful of, not a portfolio strategy. Taking both means the free month eats the hours the paid job needed. Waiting for a full rate job you have no evidence to win is how people stay at nothing for a year, and one small paid piece does not fix your price forever, because you set the next number yourself.

questions.prompt: You already moved one delivery date on this job, with notice and a reason, and the client took it well. The new date is Friday. It is Tuesday and you now know Friday is not going to happen either. What do you do?

options.text: Move the date a second time with the same notice and the same explanation you used before, since the client accepted that process without complaint the first time.
Send what exists on Friday without flagging the gaps in it, so the date is met on paper and the missing pieces follow quietly over the weekend after.
Point out that their approvals have been coming back slowly, so they can see this second slip is not really the same kind of problem as the first one was.
Tell them today, and rather than naming a third date, cut Friday's delivery down to a piece that is genuinely finished and agree the rest separately.

questions.explanation: Missing once is a slipped date. Missing twice is a client wondering whether any date you give is real, so a third date from the same source does not restore anything. Reduce what you promise until it is something you can certainly hand over, deliver that on the day you said, and treat the remainder as its own commitment. Sending incomplete work without saying so is worse than being late, because now they cannot trust the delivery either. Their slow approvals may well be true and may move the date under what you agreed, but leading with it on your second miss reads as a defence rather than a plan, and it still leaves them with no work.

questions.prompt: Your agreement lists the finished graphics as the deliverable, with the balance due on delivery. The deposit is paid and the work is done. Before the balance moves, the client asks you to send the editable working files as well. What do you do?

options.text: Send them along with the finished files. They cost you nothing to attach, and refusing a small ask over a technicality turns a repeat client into a one off.
Deliver exactly what the agreement lists, say the working files were not part of it, and offer them as a separate item with a price and terms of their own.
Refuse and tell them the working files are yours to keep. They are the reason a client comes back to you instead of handing the job to somebody cheaper.
Send them once the balance has cleared. They are asking for something they will end up getting anyway, and the timing is the part you actually control here.

questions.explanation: This is a change request arriving as a favour, and the scope document is what tells you so. Name it, price it, and let the client decide, which is neither refusing nor absorbing. Handing them over free rewrites the deal after the fact and sets what the next client expects. A flat refusal with no offer sounds like you are protecting yourself rather than describing what was bought. Waiting for the balance and then sending them anyway concedes that they were included all along, and you have given away a priceable item for nothing. Who owns which files and from when is something to write down before work starts, not to work out at handover.

questions.prompt: A client pays late every single time and keeps adding work that was never agreed. You have decided you are not taking their next job. They message asking what you can start for them in September. What do you write?

options.text: A full account of what went wrong on each job so they understand the reason, and a chance to fix it before you make the decision a final one.
A quote much higher than your usual figure, so that they either pay properly for the trouble they cause you or decline it themselves and save you the message.
That you are not able to take on new work for them, that you have enjoyed working together, and that you will finish and hand over anything still open.
That you are fully booked until further notice, so the door closes without anybody having to hear a decision they might want to argue about.

questions.explanation: Ending it is a decision you have already made, so the message only has to be short, warm and final. A client you decline cleanly still refers people, and the person who briefs you today runs somewhere else next year. The itemised account invites a negotiation you do not want and reads as a complaint, since you are not asking them to change. A punitive quote risks them saying yes, which leaves you doing the work you decided against at a price you set out of irritation. Fully booked is the softest version and it is the one that is not final: it hands them a reason to ask again in October, and you will spend this same afternoon twice.

questions.prompt: You and the client have agreed the deliverables, the exclusions, the two revision rounds, the dates and a total fee, all in an email they replied to with "yes, correct". Nothing else is written anywhere. Which of these gaps will cost you money on this job first?

options.text: A line saying what is added to the fee if payment is late, so that the client has a reason to settle the invoice rather than sit on it for as long as suits them.
What triggers each payment and by when it is due, because a total with no payment points attached to it is a number and not yet an arrangement about money.
Who owns the finished work once it has been paid for, since ownership is the item that produces the argument long after the job itself has been closed.
A signature on a proper contract document, because a thread of emails is not the kind of record that either side can sensibly rely on once there is a dispute.

questions.explanation: All four are worth having. Payment is the one whose absence costs you this month: a fee with no trigger and no due date means there is no moment at which you are owed anything, so there is nothing to chase and nothing to pause. Money before work starts, milestones on a longer job and final files on payment are arrangements you propose and write down, not rules that exist on their own. Ownership sits on the same required list and it bites at handover rather than this month, which is why chapter 2 tells you to get the money terms agreed first and settle ownership in the same thread a day later. A charge for late payment is not something to invent for yourself. A confirmed email is a real record of what two people agreed, which is what an agreement is mainly for, and what would hold up anywhere formal is a question for a lawyer.

questions.prompt: Your invoice carries your name, the client's company name, a total, and your bank details. It describes the work as 'design services'. Two weeks pass with nothing, and then somebody in their finance team emails asking what the charge is actually for. What went wrong?

options.text: Nothing went wrong with it. Two weeks of quiet is just a client who has not got round to it, and what this needs is a reminder rather than a rebuilt invoice.
It should have shown the deposit paid and the running balance, so anybody opening the file can see the whole history of the job in one place.
It reached the wrong desk. Finance never sees the brief, so an invoice has to be explained by whoever asked for the work rather than read on its own terms.
It had no number to refer to, no due date, and it described the work in words that appear nowhere in the agreement finance would be checking it against.

questions.explanation: An invoice has to be payable by somebody who was not in any of your conversations. That means a number they can quote back, the due date that was agreed, and a description in the same words as the agreement so it can be matched against what was approved. 'Design services' matches nothing and stalls at the first desk it reaches. A payment history is useful but is not what stopped this one. And finance reading it on its own is the normal case rather than a mistake, which is why you ask early who pays and what they need on the document.
